flashcards.q: What are the current LTV:CAC ratio benchmarks?
flashcards.a: 3:1 is the conventional minimum viable ratio; 4:1-5:1 is considered strong (especially enterprise/post-Series B); below 2:1 signals a business model that isn't yet capital-efficient.

flashcards.q: What is CAC payback period and why does it matter more operationally than the LTV:CAC ratio?
flashcards.a: CAC / (monthly revenue per customer x gross margin %) -- months to recoup acquisition cost via contribution margin. It matters more operationally because a company can have a great ratio and still run out of cash if payback takes 18-24 months while acquiring the next cohort before the last one paid back -- it's the actual cash-flow constraint.

flashcards.q: What are current CAC payback benchmarks?
flashcards.a: Healthy B2B SaaS: 6-12 months. Elite: 80-90 days. Mid-market drifted from ~15 months (2023) to ~18 months (2026). Payback beyond 18 months usually signals real funding pressure.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't the 'near-zero marginal cost' assumption of classic SaaS gross margins transfer to AI features?
flashcards.a: AI features have real, non-trivial marginal cost per request -- inference tokens, retrieval, and especially human review scale with usage and with the model's error rate rather than approaching zero at scale. Margin can even decline as usage grows if review/escalation rates don't improve proportionally.

flashcards.q: List the four cost layers of a real AI feature's per-request cost, and which one is most consistently omitted from engineering estimates.
flashcards.a: Retrieval (vector search infra, reranking), generation (the token-priced call), evaluation (LLM-as-judge, sampled), and human review (escalated low-confidence cases). Human review is most consistently omitted and is often the LARGEST line item.

flashcards.q: In a worked RAG feature example, what multiple was the fully-loaded per-request cost versus the generation-only estimate?
flashcards.a: Roughly 3.5-7x. Generation-only was estimated at ~$0.007/request; the fully-loaded total (retrieval + generation + eval + human review) came to roughly $0.024-0.051/request.

flashcards.q: Why does human-review cost scale differently than generation cost as a model's error rate changes, and what's the implication for optimizing margin?
flashcards.a: Human review cost is driven by escalation RATE (tied to model error/uncertainty), not a fixed per-unit price -- a higher error rate directly inflates unit cost through review, often more than generation cost. The highest-leverage margin fix is usually reducing escalation rate (better calibration/retrieval) rather than negotiating token price.

flashcards.q: How does contribution margin mechanically connect to payback period, and what's a documented benchmark for the effect size?
flashcards.a: Contribution margin is the direct multiplier in payback period's denominator (CAC / (monthly revenue x margin%)) -- margin improvement directly compresses payback. Documented benchmark: moving gross margin from 72% to 78% shortens payback by roughly 4.3 months at typical SaaS unit economics.

flashcards.q: How do CAC benchmarks differ by go-to-market motion, and why does this matter when evaluating an AI feature?
flashcards.a: PLG/self-serve ~$420, mid-market/blended ~$1,680, enterprise sales-led ~$9,400 -- structurally different cost bases, not just different scale. An AI feature's economics must be evaluated against the motion-matched benchmark; blending across motions or comparing against the wrong one hides real problems.

flashcards.q: When should you run LLM-as-judge evaluation on 100% of production traffic versus sampling?
flashcards.a: 100% during a new feature's initial rollout, after a significant model/prompt change (re-establish quality baseline), or for a genuinely high-stakes surface. Once quality is stable, sample at 10-20% -- captures the same statistical signal at a fraction of the cost, since 100% eval roughly doubles the generation-layer cost.
